speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Decarbonising our energy mix is central to this.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Energy is the existential resource challenge for our generation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Singapore imports almost all our energy needs and is alternative energy disadvantaged.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We do not have the land for large solar farms, rivers for hydropower, nor sufficient wind speeds for wind turbines.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is not just an energy transition for us, but it is a transformation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Undertaking this transformation while maintaining energy security and ensuring cost-competitiveness will not be an easy feat.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But we must take on this responsibility for the sake of future generations of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: That is why we are studying all possible decarbonisation pathways.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have sought to maximise solar deployment and we have now surpassed one gigawatt-peak of installed capacity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This makes Singapore one of the most solar-dense cities in the world.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Projects to import a total of two gigawatts of low-carbon electricity from Indonesia have also progressed to an advanced stage of development and were granted Conditional Licenses.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our focus is on building capabilities to understand and to handle new technologies should any emerge as viable decarbonisation pathways.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, next year, we will appoint a lead developer for our pathfinder project for ammonia power generation and bunkering.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: More recently, we also signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement with the United States (US).

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While we have not made any decision on nuclear energy deployment, this will help us better understand the potential applicability of advanced nuclear energy technologies in Singapore's very unique context.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond new energy sources, we can capture and store our carbon emissions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are working with S Hub, an industry consortium comprising ExxonMobil and Shell, to study the viability of a cross-border carbon capture and storage (CCS) project.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have also signed a Letter of Intent with Indonesia to further discuss CCS cooperation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Lastly, high-quality carbon credits can also support our decarbonisation journey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are establishing bilateral frameworks for credits transfers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have signed two legally binding Implementation Agreements with Papua New Guinea and Ghana, as well as signed more than 15 Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs) with partners to work towards future Implementation Agreements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will press on with these efforts to decarbonise.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But let me add that until these new low-carbon energy sources are integrated into our system, we will continue to rely on natural gas to underpin our energy security and reliability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, we are proposing amendments to the Energy Market Authority of Singapore Act 2001, or EMA Act, Electricity Act 2001 and Gas Act 2001.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Bill introduces six key proposals that will strengthen our ability to plan for and develop a decarbonised, secure and cost-competitive energy system despite the many geopolitical, commercial and technological uncertainties in our journey towards net-zero.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The first three proposals support our infrastructure planning and development for the energy transition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As we integrate different energy sources into our grid, our infrastructure will become more diverse.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There will be new terminals, cables, pipelines and substations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Many of these projects will be first-of-a-kind in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Clean energy investments may involve high upfront costs and significant commercial, technological and geopolitical risks.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, our first proposal establishes the Future Energy Fund (FEF) to provide catalytic funding to improve the commercial viability of strategic projects undertaken by private sector players, statutory bodies and other entities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, should we need to utilise hydrogen, we may have to provide financial support to mitigate commercial risks associated with developing Singapore's first-ever hydrogen terminal.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In this instance, the FEF may be used to support the terminal's development.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have begun saving up now for these infrastructure investments to reduce the burden on future generations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This prudent approach has also been adopted in other areas such as via the Coastal and Flood Protection Fund which protects Singapore against rising sea levels.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Hence, clause 6 of the Bill amends the EMA Act to establish the FEF as a statutory fund under EMA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government will make further top-ups to the FEF when our fiscal space allows.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The FEF will focus on supporting capital expenditures and will not be used to subsidise fuel costs and recurrent expenditures.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond financial support, we will also need to optimise how new energy infrastructure is developed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Given Singapore's land constraints, there may be situations where electricity and gas licensees may need access to critical energy infrastructure owned or occupied by others.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Examples of such infrastructure include waterfront jetties and transmission cables.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Such facilities may be needed to support power generation units or for cross-border electricity imports.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, EMA possesses similar powers under section 20A of the Electricity Act but these are specific to electrical connections between transmission licensees and electricity licensees.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Licensees should, first, seek to privately negotiate access with the owners or occupiers of the required critical energy infrastructure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Both parties will be provided with 30 days to agree on the terms of access to the critical energy infrastructure, including reasonable compensation for the owners or occupiers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members of the House, issuing such a direction will be a last resort, when EMA deems that such access is necessary and is in the public interest or to ensure energy security and reliability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Furthermore, an owner or occupier who disagrees with EMA's direction can appeal to the Minister of Trade and Industry for a review.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In cases where both parties fail to agree on the terms of access to the critical energy infrastructure within 30 days, either party may also request for the Minister for Trade and Industry to establish an Appeal Panel, which will determine the reasonable terms of the agreement.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Such repurposing, if not coordinated, could potentially compromise Singapore's energy supply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, repurposing gas pipelines to export carbon for overseas sequestration could compromise our electricity supplies, if these pipelines are still needed to supply gas to Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Clauses 16 and 35 of the Bill amend the Electricity Act and Gas Act, to require persons owning, managing or controlling key electricity and gas assets to obtain approval from EMA before repurposing such infrastructure away from their original use.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In evaluating these requests, EMA will consider such persons' commercial interests, while ensuring that Singapore's energy security and system reliability is not compromised.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Any such person who disagrees with EMA's decision may appeal to the Minister for Trade and Industry for a review.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Aside from infrastructure planning and development, we will also need new market mechanisms to facilitate an orderly energy transition.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Currently, the Electricity Act and Gas Act allow EMA to recover the costs of regulating electricity and gas licensees and operating Singapore's power system.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To prepare for the energy transition, EMA will need to undertake new initiatives for energy security, for market development and decarbonisation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, the Standby Liquefied Natural Gas facility (SLF) bolstered our energy security during the energy crisis, by providing generation companies with the assurance of continued supplies of gas.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This reduced volatility in the wholesale electricity market and it gave retailers the assurance to offer electricity contracts to more consumers.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: EMA will only recover the costs for such initiatives and will not seek to make any profit.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Furthermore, EMA will seek to be targeted in implementing cost recovery for these initiatives, in line with the "user pays" principle.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members of the House, this principle is not new.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Consumers currently pay for the energy-related services they use, such as the billing and meter-reading services provided by SP Services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Households and businesses are understandably concerned about whether this proposal will increase electricity prices.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: EMA will, first, consult and will provide reasonable notice to affected consumers before introducing new rates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Minister for Trade and Industry must approve any new rates that EMA may propose.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also set up a Cost Recovery Advisory Committee that will comprise non-Government representatives, to provide the Minister with independent advice on EMA's proposals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Lastly, let me elaborate on the two proposals to safeguard our energy security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members of the House, if you recall, the global energy crisis in 2021 highlighted the vulnerabilities of our current gas procurement framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, insufficient gas may be contracted under the current framework, particularly during a crisis when market conditions are uncertain.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, generation companies tend to make similar contracting decisions in response to movements in the gas market.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This leads to bunching of contracts, which magnifies Singapore's risk exposure, especially when markets are volatile.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We can learn from the approaches in other jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Japan's Energy for a New Era (JERA) and the Korea Gas Corporation (KOGAS) are responsible for procuring a significant portion of Japan's and South Korea's gas supplies.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Clause 18 of the Bill amends the Electricity Act to require prescribed power generation companies to procure gas solely from Gasco, unless otherwise allowed by EMA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Clause 25 of the Bill enables EMA to specify the minimum volume of gas that prescribed power generation companies must procure from Gasco.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Clauses 26(a), (b) and (e), 27 to 29 and 37 of the Bill, amend relevant sections of the Gas Act to, among other things, provide for centralised gas procurement as a licensable activity and grant EMA regulatory authority over Gasco.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In particular, clause 29 enables EMA to specify the volume of gas that Gasco must procure to ensure sufficient gas supplies for Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Notwithstanding our efforts on Gasco, we ultimately still depend on imports of natural gas to generate electricity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: What if we encounter a severe and protracted disruption to our gas imports?

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, there was a risk of gas supply disruptions during the energy crisis in 2021, before EMA took proactive steps to secure our fuel supply and stabilise our electricity market.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, we have a comprehensive suite of contingency measures, including system buffers, fuel reserves, voluntary power conservation, along with other pre-emptive responses, to ensure reliable and stable electricity supply.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But we should still be prepared for the unexpected, when we might need to adopt power rationing to maintain power system stability in a crisis.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Other jurisdictions, like the United Kingdom, have also incorporated power rationing as part of their energy resilience strategy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: What will happen when power rationing becomes necessary?

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, as much advance notice will be provided as possible, so that households and businesses can take actions to minimise disruptions to their activities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, we will give priority to services that are critical to Singapore's security, economic and social needs, such as medical and telecommunications services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also ensure that residents continue to have access to power for their daily needs even as we prioritise other critical facilities, such as hospitals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Third, power rationing will be lifted once these measures are no longer required for system stability.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Businesses are, understandably, concerned about the impact of power rationing.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I want to reiterate and reassure Members of the House: power rationing is only a last resort.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is one part of Singapore's preparation for an increasingly uncertain world and I hope we will never have to use it.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Lastly, the Bill also includes various miscellaneous amendments to the Electricity Act, the Gas Act and the EMA Act.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These amendments involve aligning ownership controls imposed on designated licensees with those imposed on critical firms from other sectors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Other amendments update key provisions and definitions in the Acts to support EMA's functions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: (In Mandarin):   We need to transition to clean energy whilst maintaining energy security and ensuring cost competitiveness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We cannot predict all the curveballs that may arise as we navigate the uncertainties in our decarbonisation journey.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We introduced the Energy Transition Measures and Other Amendments Bill to ensure that our regulatory framework for energy markets and infrastructure future-red.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The provisions in the Bill will ensure that our energy system remains adaptable and resilient amid uncertainties and the evolving landscape.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government remains committed to helping households with utility costs and supporting businesses in improving energy efficiency. : To conclude, this Bill strengthens our regulatory framework for energy markets and infrastructure, so that our energy system remains resilient, adaptable and aligned with our decarbonisation plans, amidst an evolving and uncertain global energy landscape.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even with the energy transition, our mission remains unchanged.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will always seek to strike an optimal balance between energy security, sustainability and cost competitiveness.

speaker: The Second Minister for Trade and Industry (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We welcome all Singaporeans and businesses to join us in this journey of advancing Singapore's energy story.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The task is made more arduous for a small island state with no natural resources and alternatives deprived.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Even to tap solar power has its limits because of our land space and the frequent cloud cover.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Climate change, geopolitics, economic nationalism, among others, have added further challenges to this formidable task of achieving energy security and resilience.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This Bill looks to beef up the current regulatory regime and addresses the all-important issue of system resilience and our ability to respond to shocks and disruptions in the supply of energy and in the energy prices.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Some may have forgotten that we actually faced an energy crisis in 2021-2022, due to the rapid economic rebound as the world emerged from the pandemic.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Of course, the crisis escalated dramatically in February 2022 when the Russian-Ukraine war broke out.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: During that crisis in November 2021, the House passed a Bill to empower EMA to acquire, build, own and operate power infrastructure to safeguard our energy security and reliability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Bill also additionally empowers EMA to impose energy and carbon efficiency on operators licensed under the Electricity Act.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Obviously, those provisions in that Bill, then, were still insufficient.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And hence, today's Bill on the Energy Transition Measures and Other Amendments.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: If we leave it to individual generation companies (gencos) to purchase the gas purely based on their commercial consideration, we may not meet the overall gas needs of the country as well as the needed security, whether it is the security of supply or price stability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To negotiate for more favourable contracting terms in the energy markets, where we are a price-taker, having considerable order size helps.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To ensure energy resilience, we should also avoid a situation where the individual procurements by gencos primarily come from the same source and, hence, subject us to concentration risk.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Having a centralised aggregator that procure with the national interest in mind, can better achieve supply source diversification.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: With scale, it will also come with better risk warehousing capabilities, which would, in turn, help manage longer-term price and supply stability.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To better manage risk, the Gasco may need to enter into longer-tenure gas supply contracts and employ forward-hedging strategies to mitigate price volatility.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We will have market situations where we lock in longer-term gas contracts, which will cost more than spot price or the short-tenure contracts.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The point here is that, there will be cost implications for a more secure and resilient energy supply.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Here, I want to ask the Minister, how would EMA continue to ensure price transparency and how would the regulator determine the transfer price between the Gasco and the gencos?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: When the Government caveats statements, such as on cost recovery, the concern, naturally, is that energy prices will be priced up and, hence, passed on to businesses and to the mass consumers.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I also seek clarity or an indication from the Minister, how significant will the cost recovery be relative to its current baseline and what are the mitigating measures?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can the FEF, which helps to initially fund new infrastructure investments, be able to help mitigate and reduce cost recovery?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Owners of electricity and gas infrastructure assets will also be required to seek EMA's approval if they plan to repurpose their assets.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is to ensure that energy security and system reliability will not be compromised.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: It will require wider engagement and education with the stakeholders and public on how this will be done and what are the likely prioritisation plans.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: I believe businesses and the public can understand the need for power rationing in an exigency situation.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: They just need to know the format that it will be done so that they can be better prepared.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Businesses also need to have some legal cover from potential liabilities as the power rationing may impact their ability to fulfil contractual obligations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I hope the Minister can also share more details on this.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Energy infrastructure investments are massive capital expenditure items and come with considerable risks, especially when we invest in new sources of energy with nascent technologies.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The investment horizons are usually much longer and the projects can cut across jurisdictions and, hence, also come with significant geopolitical risks.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: On their own, private sectors will often not be able to undertake these investments and to underwrite its entire project risk.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The FEF will come in useful and can help catalyse investments in innovative energy technologies and also put us in a better position to get the projects off the ground.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: To achieve longer-term energy security and resilience requires massive investments in energy infrastructure and, therefore, do come at a cost.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The fund is a key piece of our strategy in securing our energy future and meeting our 2050 Net Zero Objective and we support its creation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The fund is meant to catalyse the development of clean energy infrastructure in the region, through the development of infrastructure necessary for low-carbon projects that typically face high upfront capital expenditures and commercial or geopolitical risks.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: My speech today would cover three areas: the mechanics of the fund, accountability and the energy environment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Implementation refers to details about fund management, investment criteria and how the fund's mandate links to our broader energy and climate goals.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Accountability refers to clarity on stakeholders who are responsible for the fund's performance and how to benchmark the effectiveness of the fund.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Lastly, our energy environment refers to wider trends that affect the decarbonisation of our energy mix.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, we would need an exponential increase in renewables between just 2030 and 2035 alone.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I have some clarifications relating to the implementation of the fund.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As with most capital-intensive infrastructure projects, particularly for energy projects, commissioning times before such projects even begin yielding outcomes play a critical role.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In a 2024 study on renewable energy project, globally-funded by the European Union's Horizon 2020 Research and Innovation Programme under the European Research Council, commissioning times across renewable technologies and regions have increased on average between 2015 and 2022.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The same paper called for more policy interventions to address this increase in times, ranging from insulating projects from fiscal shocks to standardising legal processes surrounding projects.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given also, that target projects supported by the fund can include nascent technologies, these being one of the factors that increases commissioning time, how does the Government plan to use the fund to address potentially lengthy commissioning times and how does it see the efficacy of using the fund to meet our 2035 targets?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Also on the mechanics of the fund, I note that the proposed new section 19A(1)(a) uses the wording "any low-carbon energy project or energy supply security project".

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Does this mean that the fund could, hypothetically, support a new built fossil fuel project in the name of energy security?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would any project qualify, as long as it meets the criteria of being necessitated by any low-carbon energy project as described in 19A(6)?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I note that power back-up is explicitly given as an example in 19A(6)(b), but could this also mean support for fossil fuel power stations providing baseload power?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What are the scenarios where the fund would support fossil fuel power for non-back-up use?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Would the Minister confirm that the fund will not be used to rely on fossil fuels as a crutch, especially if it means that we are stuck with using this crutch in the long term?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A query I have is, what happens if projects are terminated early?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In the case of the 100-megawatt Lao DPR-Thailand-Malaysia-Singapore Power Integration Project (LTMS-PIP), it was reported that the deal is currently on pause over government-level disagreements.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What happens if assets supported by the fund are stranded due to project failures or pauses?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As we work towards these national energy goals, accountability allows us to equip accountable stakeholders with commensurate mandates and authority to see through the successful implementation of these targets.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We fall short of targets when lines of accountability are unclear or if our strategic approach is flawed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We need to learn from our experiences in the arena of food insecurity, specifically, the difficulties faced in achieving our "30 by 30" goal, in working to achieve our goal for energy security in the coming decade and beyond.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We can also learn from the failures of investing in unproven technologies, as was the case in the US.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The 2009 American Recovery and Reinvestment Act offered US$3.4 billion for the research and development of carbon capture and sequestration projects.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A case study of 11 demonstration projects selected by the US Department of Energy, resulted in only two continuing to remain operational.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: A further five commercial projects saw only one reaching operational implementation, which eventually closed within four years.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In this example, the failure of capital deployed can be attributed to the lack of financial viability of a range of carbon capture technologies, a risk that cannot be overlooked when dealing with nascent technologies.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In view of this, I have some clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Funds typically appoint a designated fund manager or have a general partner responsible for evaluating projects, investment decisions and the overall management of fund operations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Which agency will be the fund manager for the FEF?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On a broader level, which Ministry or agency holds ultimate accountability for our target energy mix and transition to 30% renewable sources by 2035?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On an explicit strategic approach and fund objectives, what does success for the fund look like?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given that our country’s energy security and transition are fundamentally critical to our survival, how will this translate into the fund balancing between the need for financial returns versus the long-term strategic costs necessary for such a transition?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Can the Minister clarify what are our key performance indicators (KPIs) for the fund?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Aside from supporting the 2035 target for six gigawatts target for low-carbon imports which will provide 30% of Singapore’s electricity supply, will the impact on the grid emission factor, which calculates the actual climate impact of the changes, be a KPI?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moving on to more general points about our energy environment and maximising the climate impact of the fund.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As we ramp up towards transitioning our energy mix, our energy demand has been growing consistently.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: With industrial usage set for significant growth, especially from energy-intensive use cases, such as data centres, necessitated by the growth of artificial intelligence (AI) applications, it is likely that total energy demand will grow more.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While we may be able to achieve our target of 30% renewables, the wider challenge remains.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We are already seeing power-hungry AI applications drive outsized demand for energy just to keep data centres running.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Given our AI ambitions, we have been looking for “clean” sources in the region to meet demand, including solar farms in Australia and wind or hydropower sources from our ASEAN neighbours – Malaysia, Vietnam, Laos, for instance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, what happens when our ASEAN neighbours start requiring a significant amount of renewables to power their own transition and development?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: What, too, do we do if geopolitical conflict results in energy supply lines being cut, such as was the case with the Nord Stream natural gas pipelines?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our regulations and policies are also important in boosting Singapore’s energy security which, in turn, will affect our geopolitical risk tolerance with electricity imports.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But with an economic lifespan of around 25 years, is there a timeline for these power plants to run on green zero-emission hydrogen?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If these fossil fuel plants are unable to meet net-zero power, will they be retired early to make way for low-carbon imports?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And in terms of domestic consumption, unlike electricity generated overseas, we have some control over our electricity consumption.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Ultimately, the drive for successfully transitioning our energy sources and decarbonisation will require us to not just pay attention to supply, but also demand.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We cannot neglect to continue to raise awareness of energy conservation and wider sustainability concerns, and both industry and households have to continue to work together, keeping our energy use in check.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This would not only cut emissions and electricity costs but will also provide some options in our energy security.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: A confluence of factors, including the war in Ukraine, supply chain disruptions and gas production shortages, caused electricity prices to soar.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And when electricity prices go up, business costs went up and our domestic food prices also went up.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Bill focuses on one of our four supply “switches” – how we make our natural gas generators more efficient.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I have some clarifications and comments on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Seeing the Ministry of Trade and Industry's (MTI’s) stated objectives for the Bill, I cannot help but think of the usual saying about the “impossible trinity”: fast, cheap and good.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: You can usually only have two out of the three.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, when we are seeking to decarbonise in line with our international commitments and our own green plans and to diversify so as to ensure our energy security, it would seem quite impossible to decrease prices and keep our costs competitive.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Some increase in price seems to be inevitable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: With the changes in this Bill, can the Minister share his thoughts whether Singaporeans and Singapore businesses should expect electricity prices to trend upwards in the near and medium term?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Power generation companies (gencos) would then have to buy natural gas from the CGE.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This reminds me of the establishment of the predecessor of NTUC FairPrice amidst the oil crises of the 1970s.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The consumer co-operative would buy essentials in bulk and pass the savings on to the consumers, combating profiteering at the same time.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is there already an idea of who this CGE is going to be and how it is going to be run and managed?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Will it be part of an existing Government-linked company?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I suspect it cannot be a purely private commercial enterprise since it is going to be put in a monopolistic market position vis-à-vis the gencos.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: To achieve our aim of ensuring cost competitiveness, how will the Government be able to influence the CGE to pursue non-profit maximisation objectives?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In fact, this monopolistic structure has been raised as an issue during MTI and EMA’s public consultation earlier this year.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Respondents flagged the potential loss of flexibility to procure gas from other market participants.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This not only includes different upstream gas suppliers, but also horizontal gas companies which find that they have more gas than they need.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would this not deprive gencos of the ability to capitalise on opportunistic spot liquefied natural gas (LNG) contracts to bring down their overall cost of generating electricity, which they can pass on to electricity consumers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On a free market theory, would it not be more efficient if gencos were left to search for the most competitive gas supplier and arrangement?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I note from the Ministry’s consultation responses that legacy gas contracts will not be affected by the new regulatory regime.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We know that our gencos generally rely on long-term gas contracts in order to keep electricity prices relatively stable.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Do we have any idea what is the rundown period for these existing contracts, before they need to start to purchase from, or through, the CGE?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Next, is there also a contradiction when we seek to use the CGE to aggregate natural gas demands and achieve economies of scale in procurement and our other aim to enhance our energy security by procuring from multiple, diversified sources?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How many different countries do our gencos import our gas from?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the maximum percentage of our total gas imports that come from a single country?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the FEF subsume existing initiatives for the uptake of clean and efficient energy solutions?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The official press release for the introduction of this Bill stated that the proposed amendments to the Electricity Act and the Gas Act will allow EMA to recover costs from entities and persons who benefit from these initiatives.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is quite unclear how these cost recovery powers are intended to be used.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can the Minister give examples of when and how these cost recovery powers might be used?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: When it comes to energy assets and infrastructure, the first change is to require owners of key electricity and gas assets to obtain the EMA’s prior approval before repurposing such assets.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More fundamentally, has there be any particular incident in the past few years which has sparked this concern around repurposing?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The other material change is the EMA’s power to direct owners of critical energy infrastructure to enter an agreement with licensees for access to the critical energy infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This power may seem overreaching as it intrudes upon the infrastructure owner’s freedom to contract or not to contract with a particular party.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Before this, EMA was previously given power to direct gencos to generate electricity using gas from the SLF.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the licensee and the infrastructure owner cannot agree on the terms upon which the licensee would have access, either party may request the Minister for Trade and Industry to establish an Appeal Panel to determine the reasonable terms for the agreement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But 10 reasonable persons can come up with 10 different reasonable proposals.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, what are the factors that the Appeal Panel will consider and refer to in determining the “reasonable terms” of the forced agreement?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would subsidiary legislation be passed for this purpose?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In determining what terms would be “reasonable”, would the Appeal Panel be able to access the terms of other agreements entered into by the owner of the critical infrastructure giving access to other licensees?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The problem is that most of these agreements and their terms would probably be commercially sensitive and subject to express confidentiality obligations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But it is difficult to think of our resilient and sustainable energy strategy without considering the other three supply “switches” as well.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is it realistic to set even more ambitious targets for our solar deployment?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, how many are already in the pipeline and in the midst of works?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How much has already been spent on the planning and infrastructure, including for plans that have been abandoned due to subsequent developments?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: On that note, Mr Speaker, Sir, notwithstanding the clarifications sought, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Our dependence on imports for almost all our energy makes us highly vulnerable to external shocks.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In the face of these challenges, the measures proposed in this Bill are both timely and essential.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, we have witnessed unprecedented volatility in energy markets.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Since then, such spikes have become more frequent, with surges as high as 3,000% in 2023, despite a sharp decline in LNG prices.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This volatility underscores how vulnerable we are to global energy fluctuations, and it is essential that we take steps to mitigate these risks.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The spikes in electricity prices have had a significant impact on both households and businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In a tight labour market where wages are rising and supply chain pressures persist, the added uncertainty of fluctuating energy costs has become a major concern for businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: According to Singapore Business Federation's Business Survey 2023/2024, rising business costs, particularly in the areas of wages, pass through from suppliers, and electricity costs, are among the top challenges that businesses face today.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, this Bill offers much relief by addressing some of the systemic issues contributing to these rising costs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Centralising gas procurement through the establishment of the CGE, as proposed, will enhance efficiency and provide stability in gas supply which, in turn, will help stabilise prices.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, the amendments that empower EMA to facilitate access to critical infrastructure, approve the repurposing of critical assets, and implement power rationing during emergencies are crucial to maintaining the reliability of our system.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This framework is welcomed by businesses as it ensures operational continuity and energy supply reliability, both of which are critical to our long-term success.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, I would like to seek clarification regarding the establishment of the CGE.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As it stands, we have licensed gas aggregators, including SembCorp, ExxonMobil, Shell, Pavilion and Keppel, which manage gas procurement and supply.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These entities are already tasked with demand aggregation, diversifying energy sources and ensuring sufficient gas supply for our power needs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister clarify how the CGE will succeed in achieving these goals where the current aggregators may have faced challenges?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: What specific issues or gaps have been identified with the existing framework and how will the CGE address these challenges more effectively to ensure energy stability and security for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, for Singapore to achieve its net-zero emissions target by 2050, we must prioritise decarbonisation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The FEF will support low-carbon energy technologies, which are necessary for our energy transition which the private sector may find it difficult to manage on its own.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It may consider supporting large-scale cross-border solar projects, such as the recently announced one gigawatt AC solar energy import from Indonesia, where grid charges and backup fees are already imposed by EMA to maintain grid stability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These projects require significant Battery Energy Storage Systems to store daytime energy for nighttime transmission, and collaboration with host countries is crucial for their success.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: If FEF supports these initiatives, its investments in subsea cables and cross-border infrastructure will be instrumental in realising their potential and accelerating Singapore's decarbonisation efforts.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While businesses understand the importance of enhancing energy security and supporting decarbonisation, I must emphasise that cost recovery measures outlined in the Bill should not exacerbate the cost pressures businesses are already facing.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As we work towards energy resilience, it is crucial that the cost recovery mechanisms are implemented fairly, transparently and in a sustainable manner.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Any additional cost burdens must be carefully considered to avoid undermining their competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: In light of this, I would like to propose four key recommendations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: First, transparency is paramount in determining how costs are calculated and allocated to licensees and consumers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I am glad to hear from the Minister that EMA will form a cost recovery committee and recommend that this panel will have representation from businesses and industry players to assess how costs are allocated.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This will ensure that the costs are distributed fairly, preventing any undue burden on businesses and consumers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, I recommend a phased approach to cost recovery.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses need sufficient runway to adjust to any changes in cost structures, especially in today's economic climate.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A gradual implementation of cost recovery measures will prevent sudden financial shocks.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, to further support businesses and maintain their competitiveness, a cap on the maximum allowable cost recovery in any given year could be introduced to mitigate financial strain.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Third, while renewable energy is vital for decarbonisation, we must recognise the costs associated with its intermittency.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The "user pays" principle has been a core part of Singapore's solar energy project planning for over a decade.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As we expand beyond two GWp, the intermittency costs will grow and renewable energy producers should share in the responsibility for maintaining grid stability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This principle ensures that we fairly distribute the costs across all stakeholders in the energy ecosystem.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, for a more holistic approach to energy security, I urge the Government to include renewable energy imports as part of our energy supply strategy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A centralised entity similar to the CGE could be established to manage the procurement of renewable energy.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This would complement our broader energy diversification efforts and strengthen our overall energy security while also accelerating the transition to a cleaner energy future.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I have several further clarifications to seek from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These systems are increasingly important for energy storage and ensuring efficiency in power usage.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, while facilitating access to critical infrastructure is important, we must ensure that it is done carefully.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, like to seek clarifications on the conditions under which licensees may gain access to this infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Mandating that a business provide access to its competitors could risk eroding its value and competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is essential that any such regulations balance the need for collaboration with the protection of business interests.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Clear guidelines and criteria are essential to prevent disputes and ensure that compensation is fair.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Moreover, in the event of a disagreement between parties, will there be a formal resolution process to ensure that the disputes are handled reasonably, efficiently and fairly?

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Third, the Bill gives EMA the power to implement power rationing during emergencies, which is a necessary safeguard.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, it is critical that EMA provide clear definitions of what constitutes an emergency.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses need to understand to what extent their liabilities are limited due to power rationing and the protocols that will be in place to ensure that essential services remain operational and disruptions are minimised.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I also recommend that a robust communication mechanism be established so that affected businesses are promptly informed about the initiation, duration and cessation of power rationing measures.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: As we move forward, it is crucial that Singapore not only meets its Green Plan 2030 targets but also positions itself as a global leader in sustainability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Embracing new energy technologies, such as solar, wind and hydrogen, will not only reduce our carbon footprint but also enhance our energy security and bolster our economy's resilience.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To expedite progress in these areas, we must ensure that our regulations are flexible enough to keep pace with the evolving energy landscape.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Aligning safety regulations with those of leading solar economies could be a key step in the right direction.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, for businesses that have yet to start their green transition, the Government could consider introducing building-level incentives to encourage the adoption of sustainability infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This could involve clustering tenants in properties specifically designed to support green initiatives, which could lower barriers to adoption and spur greater investment in sustainable technologies.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This initiative is focused on helping businesses adapt to sustainability and decarbonisation efforts.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: AfA will soon release our recommendations aimed at enhancing business competitiveness while maintaining momentum towards decarbonisation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This work aligns closely with the objectives of this Bill, ensuring that businesses remain competitive and resilient as we advance towards our energy and sustainability goals.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Stabilising electricity costs will be crucial to maintaining Singapore's long-term competitiveness in a rapidly evolving global landscape.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The proposed amendments seek to enhance Singapore's regulatory regime for energy markets and related infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Singapore imports most of our fuel, which makes us vulnerable to global supply and demand shifts and price fluctuations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While Singapore has worked hard to strengthen our energy resilience, the supply disruptions and volatility experienced during the 2021/2022 global energy crisis has highlighted the need for further safeguards to ensure Singapore's energy security.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With increasing digitalisation and economic growth, our energy needs will only further increase.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The challenges brought about by climate change have driven our ambition to achieve net-zero by 2050.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To do this, we need to transition, or as the Minister has said, to transform, to renewable energy.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While I am supportive of the proposed amendments in the Bill, I do wish to seek clarifications on three of the proposed amendments: first, the FEF; second, centralised gas procurement; and third, cost recovery.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: EMA and MTI have highlighted that such energy sources will likely involve nascent technologies, large-scale projects that require higher capital expenditures and exposure to significant commercial and geopolitical risks.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I support the setting up of the FEF as it is crucial that Singapore invests in, builds know-how and taps on new sources of low-carbon energy for the transition of our power sector and for our energy security.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While the set-up of the FEF is important, I would like to understand how the FEF will encourage and attract the right investments and what are the criteria on which projects will be selected for funding.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While the Minister did say that there will be no limit on what we study and all the possible low-carbon energy projects and sources, and while the technology is also very nascent, I would ask if we have identified promising technologies that are aligned with our larger energy masterplan, given the fact that our runway is really quite short.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This transition will require investments, infrastructure upgrades and enhancements.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This may lead to higher energy and electricity prices.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is a point I will discuss in my later clarification on cost recovery.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The amendment will require power generation companies to procure gas solely from the Gasco and to empower EMA to regulate the Gasco.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As outlined by the Minister in his speech, with demand aggregation, the intent is to derive cost competitive benefits for our gas supply, diversify our energy sources and ensure sufficient supply of gas to meet our power needs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The centralisation of gas procurement will reduce the flexibility of the power generation companies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Therefore, the success of the Gasco in achieving its mandate is critical for Singapore's energy security and price competitiveness.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: On that point, I would like to seek an understanding of how EMA will measure the Gasco's effectiveness in securing sufficient gas supply for our power needs and in providing competitive pricing to the power generation companies.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The cost recovery will be from entities and persons who benefit from the initiatives or services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This will increase cost for the entities and persons and, possibly, lead to higher energy and electricity prices.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can the Minister share more information on what would trigger the decision for the need for such cost recovery, the framework for such cost recovery and the lead time that will be provided to both organisations and households that cost will be recovered from?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It requires strong commitment and action from all stakeholders and not just the Government.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The efforts are not straightforward and will take time to achieve.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The proposed amendments in the Bill are timely.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But how we move forward and execute is equally important.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As the world grapples with the challenges of climate change and the finite nature of fossil fuels, economies around the globe are increasingly transitioning towards more sustainable sources of energy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This shift is driven by a need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, enhance energy security and future-proof economies against the volatility of traditional energy markets.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: For us in Singapore, energy transition is not just an environmental imperative but an economic necessity, too.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: As a small, resource-constrained country with limited availability of renewable energy resources within, Singapore is highly dependent on imported energy, notably natural gas.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The volatility of the global energy markets, as evidenced by the global energy crisis of 2021-2022, poses significant risks to the country's energy security and economic stability.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: By transitioning towards more sustainable energy sources, such as solar power, low-carbon hydrogen and regional renewable energy imports, Singapore can reduce its reliance on fossil fuels, enhance its energy resilience and contribute to global efforts to combat climate change.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, embracing this transition offers Singapore the opportunity to position itself as a leader in clean energy innovation in Southeast Asia, potentially driving economic growth through new industries and technologies.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: The provisions in this Bill bring about numerous opportunities for Singapore businesses and the Singapore economy as a whole.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: This positions Singapore as a leader in green energy and contributes to global climate goals.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In turn, this will attract investment in renewable energy projects and related technologies into our economy.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, focusing on low-carbon energy projects opens opportunities for businesses to venture into renewable energy, energy storage and related technologies and allows for companies that innovate in these areas to tap into new markets and revenue streams.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Regions, like the European Union and the Americas, faced severe impacts from oil, gas and electricity shortages during the global energy crisis of 2021-2022.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Thanks to the quick actions taken by MTI and EMA, Singapore avoided electricity supply disruptions during that period by leveraging on existing system buffers.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Building on this experience, the Bill seeks to further enhance energy reliability, which is essential for economic stability and growth.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: One, one area of concern are the associated regulatory changes and the cost of implementation of these regulatory changes, particularly for businesses that rely heavily on energy as an input.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs, especially, may face significant costs during the transition, including investing in new technology, complying with the regulations and dealing with potential disruptions.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Also, industries dependent on traditional energy sources will encounter higher expenses and operational challenges as they shift to low-carbon alternatives.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: These costs could include investments in new technology, compliance with new regulations and potential disruptions during the transition.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister please provide us with a comprehensive update on the support measures available for SMEs?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Three, under what specific circumstances would EMA initiate electricity rationing?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: In case of rationing, how will affected businesses and consumers be notified and what measures are in place to minimise disruptions?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, are there any plans to conduct electricity rationing drills to familiarise industries with what to do when it happens, just like the regular fire drills that our buildings conduct?

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, I seek the Minister's views on the legislation's impact on existing contracts.

speaker: Mr Neil Parekh Nimil Rajnikant (Nominated Member)
text: How will the Bill affect existing contracts between energy suppliers and consumers, especially if new regulations or rationing measures are introduced?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I believe the Bill's proposals are absolutely necessary and are heartened that we are doing this now to improve Singapore's energy regulatory framework to safeguard our energy security.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: However, I have some clarifications and a few suggestions.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: How do we ensure the logic, which underpins our energy strategy, remains sound?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: There is always a risk that well-intended improvements to an existing framework will be built on existing and, sometimes, entrenched mindsets, which may be less relevant for a changed context.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The energy sector and the context that it exists in, is evolving rapidly with a very fast-changing technology landscape.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For a huge endeavour like energy transition that invariably takes time, we need to constantly check if our mindsets and accompanying approaches remain appropriate each step of the way.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I would, therefore, like to clarify: how does the Government ensure that our energy security policies remain relevant with the ever-shifting and emerging contexts and technologies and that, we are not, as the saying goes, "training to fight the last war"?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: For example, as its name suggests, the establishment of the FEF could be absolutely necessary to experiment with new approaches.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: It supports the development and trialling of emerging technology to make energy production and transmission more efficient.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We also need evidence from these experiments to improve our strategy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: My question is: how do we also provide safeguards to prevent decision-makers from merely, so-called, "following the money"?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: How do we avoid getting caught up in areas where capital injections and investments are flowing and assume that it works simply because it is "high growth"?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: When, ultimately, it may be scientifically unsound or inappropriate?

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: One only needs to look at our experience with high-tech farming to see the possibility of this pitfall.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Not that many years ago, many private as well as state investors began putting their money in high-tech farming in a bid to solve food security issues amidst global warming.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: But recent developments have shown that, a high growth area in terms of capital and investments do not necessarily provide the desired results.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We should also bear this in mind, in considering our energy investments strategy.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Solar energy, for example, has been held up as a renewable, low-carbon and, therefore, a better source of electricity.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: However, if we consider its full cost of generation, transmission and storage, solar energy wins in some areas, but fails in many others.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Solar energy still faces the same transmission inefficiencies as other sources.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Large solar panels and high-capacity storage batteries required to generate and store at a commercially-viable scale, require huge quantities of rare resources that require us to further excavate and exploit the Earth.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The overall infrastructure required is also energy-intensive and we cannot exclude these costs from our calculations.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The fact is, until a technological breakthrough dawns upon humanity to unlock viable alternative sources of affordable energy, it will remain expensive, unless global demand somehow does a cliff drop drastically.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Looking at the emergence of AI and the number of data centres required and the amount of electricity and energy consumed by these data centres, I do not see this cliff drop happening anytime soon.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Given Singapore’s land constraints that make existing renewable energy sources unimplementable for us, we will continue to depend on deals with other countries for our electricity supply.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This makes us vulnerable to conditions that affect their willingness to supply to us.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We can infer that if they can get a better deal out of us, they will!

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Achieving energy security, therefore, necessitates that we do not look only at “supply side” solutions, but also at “demand side” solutions.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: To ensure Singaporeans are resilient in a worst case scenario, we must shift from focusing on energy efficiency and expecting cheaper energy to simply getting used to using less and, potentially, having less.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Minister Tan See Leng took pains earlier to stress that power rationing will be a last resort measure and I can imagine he is very concerned about the implications on business and economic activity.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Categories of “essential activities” and “non-essential activities” could be created to educate the public about the amount of electricity they consume.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: This can be a nationwide exercise and take in the comments, feedback and inputs from all citizens.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: The effort could even be gamified, the same way that the Health Promotion Board did with the National Steps Challenge, to help us develop a habit of moving more for better health and now we can do “Using Less for Better Resilience”.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Such campaigns will help citizens develop a perspective on what are energy essentials and what are non-essential in their lives, paving the way to, possibly, setting electricity budgets for different categories of activities in future.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: We need not wait for a crisis to happen to begin our efforts towards energy sufficiency and to develop a more accurate perspective of our collective reliance on electricity.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I will speak more about air-conditioning in the next debate on the Building Control (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I do not envy the Ministries and all the personnel involved who are tasked to find solutions to our energy resilience.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Nevertheless, I have faith that as a people, Singaporeans are adaptable and pragmatic.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Even though I expect there will be many complaints and pushback from segments of society about just the idea of rationing electricity, I believe we have the creativity, gumption and cohesion at the end of the day, to do what is pragmatic and necessary.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: And instead of offering just a doom-and-gloom picture, I would like to offer a nice vision to accompany what some people might viscerally reject as a first reaction towards electricity rationing.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Create a window of time for families to get out to nature to play and to bond.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Learn to get to destinations again without global positioning system which by the way helps us to train and develop the hippocampus part in our brains!

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Go to the beach and enjoy the sea breeze instead of the aircon!

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Or have heart-to-heart talks without digital distractions being available.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: Maybe husbands and wives can start looking into each other's eyes again over dinner.

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: In the space created by non-access to digital and electronically enabled entertainment, maybe Singaporeans may make even more babies – I hope!

speaker: Ms Carrie Tan (Nee Soon)
text: I believe Singaporeans can be empowered to do our parts to preemptive education and sensitisation.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Singaporeans' livelihoods and well-being depend very much on the provision of reliable and affordable energy.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: As we work to decarbonise and reach net zero emissions by 2050, our energy profile will go through significant change.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is important to recognise that the energy transition is not just about reducing emissions but is also central to ensuring long-term sustainability.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: By shifting towards cleaner energy sources, we can safeguard our environmental resources for future generations while enhancing energy resilience.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This transition aligns with our broader sustainability goals by reducing the harmful impacts of fossil fuels, improving air quality and fostering the development of green technologies that will sustain both economic growth and ecological balance.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this way, energy security and environmental sustainability are inextricably linked, making it critical for us to act decisively in accelerating this transition.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While the gas procurement through the CGE is limited to gas users from the power sector, such as generation companies, the concerns over the potential risks and vulnerabilities from centralisation remain valid.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On one hand, the aggregate demand will give us more bargaining power, achieve better pricing and greater efficiencies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: On the other hand, how will the Government ensure that the CGE does not become a bottleneck or a single point of failure in our energy supply chain?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What contingency plans are in place should the CGE encounter difficulties in securing adequate gas supplies?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would the Ministry consider establishing an independent oversight body to monitor the CGE’s performance, thereby mitigating the risks of centralisation?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I would also like to suggest that Government ensure the diversification of gas supply sources by setting limits on the proportion of gas bought from various suppliers.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Mandarin):   EMA’s cost recovery framework can potentially lead to increased energy costs for consumers, which might disproportionately impact lower-income households or smaller businesses that are already operating on tight margins.
