speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What safeguards are in place to ensure that these cost recovery mechanisms do not unduly burden consumers, particularly those who are most vulnerable?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will transparency be maintained throughout this process?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is imperative that we protect those who are least able to absorb additional costs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, what is the expected impact of decarbonisation exercises on our energy costs, which must remain competitive enough to attract big multinational corporations to set up operations in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Is there a standardised mechanism and framework being considered to ensure fair compensation and avoid prolonged disagreements?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Prolonged disputes could result in service disruptions or increased costs that would ultimately trickle down to the end users, including our most vulnerable citizens.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Regarding the requirement for approval when repurposing existing energy infrastructure, I am concerned about the problem of bureaucratic delays.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While oversight is necessary to ensure our energy security and reliability, we must also ensure that it does not hinder the agility of companies in responding to market changes.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What will be the thresholds and will the criteria be reviewed periodically?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How will EMA ensure that rationing measures are proportionate and do not unduly disrupt our economic activities?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure that any rationing is fair and does not disadvantage those already struggling to make ends meet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As part of Singapore’s strategy to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050, this Bill is a positive move that supports decarbonisation whilst ensuring energy security and keeping power costs competitive for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have four points for clarification to raise.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share more details on how this sum of $5 billion was derived?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share the time frame for the utilisation of the initial $5 billion sum?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The cost of mitigation and adaptation is likely to rise steeply as the impact of climate change intensifies over the next century.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When does the Government expect to have to make the next injection?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Government anticipate making smaller and more frequent future injections or relatively infrequent but large injections?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: EMA also announced in its media release that the Government will ensure prudent use of the funds and oversight over projects.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister provide more details on the safeguards that will be put in place to ensure transparency and public accountability on the use of the funds in the future by the EMA?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on the establishment of the CGE.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: During the public consultation, EMA clarified that the centralised gas procurement regime will only apply to gas users from the power sector such as generation companies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: EMA said that non-power sector consumers such as industrial gas users will be excluded.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The rationale of stabilising gas supply through centralised gas procurement is undermined if the excluded non-power sector consumers and legacy gas contracts form a substantial portion of gas demand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also share more details on the CGE’s pricing framework and how the contracts between the CGE and generation companies will be negotiated?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MTI and EMA stated during the public consultation that the amendments will empower EMA to introduce gas procurement terms on generation companies such as minimum gas contracting obligations to ensure they contract sufficient fuel.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will these gas procurement terms be consistent across the board or will the CGE be imposing differentiated terms based on independently negotiated contracts with the generation companies?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: EMA has also stated that one of its aims is to keep gas prices low and competitive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share how prices will be kept competitive when there is only one central gas supplier to generation companies and generation companies no longer have gas price competitiveness from varied suppliers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is on EMA’s power to make directions allowing access by licensees to electricity and gas supplies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These powers are set out under the amended section 20A of the Electricity Act and section 38B of the Gas Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The powers on the installation, use and access to key infrastructure are broad.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: EMA may even direct the licensee and any person to enter into an agreement with each other on the maintenance or use of the infrastructure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If parties are unable to agree on the terms and are unable to enter into an agreement, a party can request that the Minister for Trade and Industry establish an Appeal Panel to determine reasonable terms.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This allows the Government very exceptional powers to determine the terms of a private agreement between two parties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: During the public consultation, respondents asked about the safeguards to minimise the impact on investor confidence, reduce the burden on property owners and moderate costs for consumers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Respondents also asked about mechanisms other than EMA directives to facilitate shared access.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: EMA stated that it will only use directives if it considers such access necessary and in the public interest to ensure energy security and reliability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister share whether it will consult with parties on the potential costs and commercial risks to the parties before making such directives?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even where access is necessary and in the public interest, will EMA consider using other less restrictive measures before making directives as a last resort?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the event that loss is suffered by any party due to a term that was agreed under EMA's directive, can Minister clarify whether it is a defence or mitigating factor for the party to claim that the term was entered into because of EMA's direction or determined by an appeal panel.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final point is on the cost recovery mechanism for energy initiatives in section 19B of the EMA Act.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is some uncertainty as to how this mechanism will operate given the flexibility afforded to EMA in imposing the rate recoverable.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 19B(3) of the EMA Act permits EMA to make a "reasonable estimation" of the amount of costs that will be incurred when imposing such a rate when such amounts are yet to be determined.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Section 19B(8) allows EMA to retain any excess costs recovered and apply such excess to other energy initiatives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Further, costs can also be recovered from any consumer of energy utilities under section 19B(4)(iv).

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill marks a pivotal moment for Singapore's energy future.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill aims to reduce that reliance by shifting to cleaner energy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is a step toward a future where Singapore controls its energy destiny.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, I have several clarifications on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: First, Mr Speaker, Sir, innovation is vital, but it must come with guardrails.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we must tread carefully with investments in untested technologies.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Are we betting on the future with enough safeguards in place?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What safeguards are in place to manage these risks?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Could the Ministry also provide more details on how projects are selected for funding?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the FEF integrate with existing initiatives like the Emerging Technology Grant?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about ensuring every dollar drives real progress.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We also need to ensure that the research we fund is practical for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For example, the Directed Hydrogen Programme relies on hydrogen produced overseas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Does this align with our goal of energy independence?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Should we not focus on solutions that we can scale right here at home?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Second, Mr Speaker, Sir, transitioning to low-carbon energy should not come at the cost of social equity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We cannot let the burden of this transition fall on those least able to bear it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Has the Ministry fully assessed the impact on vulnerable groups?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill does not currently include measures to shield low-income households from energy cost increases.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many Singaporeans are already feeling the squeeze due to high cost of living.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will they bear even higher energy costs without seeing the benefits?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The long-term benefits of reducing reliance on imported fuels are clear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But we need to address the immediate impact on energy affordability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Government ensure vulnerable groups are not left behind in this transition?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Microsoft is buying solar power from public buildings in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Why is this solar energy not used to subsidise energy costs for low-income households?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When public buildings generate renewable energy, should the first priority not be the public?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, we must balance long-term sustainability with immediate needs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Supporting fast-response generators and energy storage systems is critical for grid stability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But relying too heavily on carbon-intensive systems like diesel generators could undermine our sustainability goals.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Why are these generators part of our energy mix?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does this align with our low-carbon commitments?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need a clear roadmap to phase out these stopgap measures for more sustainable solutions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fourth, Mr Speaker, Sir, transparency and public accountability are the bedrock of public trust.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The FEF, as proposed, gives the Minister significant control with some limited public oversight.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This raises concerns about how the fund will be managed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can the Minister share more details on the mechanisms to ensure transparency and public accountability in the fund's management?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Singaporeans need to trust that our resources are being used wisely and effectively.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Fifth, Mr Speaker, Sir, the Bill's impact on energy market dynamics needs clarity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The provision allowing EMA to direct key facilities could affect market fairness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, we must be careful not to stifle innovation or discourage new entrants.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What measures will prevent market distortions or monopolistic behaviour?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will the Ministry ensure EMA's expanded powers do not create an uneven playing field?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will this Bill support a truly open and competitive electricity market?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We should encourage more low-carbon energy suppliers to enter the market, giving consumers more sustainable choices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some power plant generators are owned by foreign consortiums.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How does EMA plan to work with these players to ensure fair and transparent centralised gas procurement?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will rates be standardised across all generators to ensure fairness?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Lastly, Mr Speaker, Sir, the energy sector is evolving rapidly.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure our laws evolve with it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A static framework risks being outpaced by new innovations and market realities.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What plans does the Ministry have for regular reviews or updates to this Bill?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is critical to ensure it stays relevant as technology advances.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It strengthens our energy security, supports low-carbon projects and ensures a stable, reliable energy supply.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These are key pillars for our economic stability and resilience.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill is Singapore's declaration that we are serious about tackling the global climate crisis.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It positions us as a leader in the global energy transition.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It attracts investment, creates new jobs and enhances our competitiveness in the green economy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, for this Bill to truly succeed, we must address the potential challenges it poses.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need clear safeguards for managing the risks associated with the FEF.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We must ensure social equity is not sacrificed and that vulnerable households are protected from rising energy costs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We need to prioritise long-term sustainability and phase out carbon-intensive stopgap measures.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Transparency, accountability, and market fairness are not just desirable, they are essential.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Not long ago, we imported all our water, just as we do with our energy today.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But through bold initiatives, strategic investments and a relentless focus on sustainability, we turned that vulnerability into strength.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We diversified our water supply, developed NEWater, invested in desalination and championed water conservation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, Singapore is a global model for water sustainability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The parallels with our current energy landscape are striking.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We can reduce our dependence, diversify our sources and lead the world in the transition to low-carbon energy.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Just as Singapore became a global leader in water management, we have the potential to become a beacon of energy resilience and sustainability.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Our success could inspire other nations to follow suit.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about setting a standard – one that shows the world how a small, resource-scarce nation can rise to the challenge, innovate and lead by example.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Their speeches centred around three key issues: first, electricity costs and how we will invest in our energy future; second, safeguards to EMA's powers; and third, the implementation approach for power rationing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Before addressing these questions, let me reiterate the purpose of this Bill.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As Mr Yip Hong Weng, Mr Mark Lee and Ms Carrie Tan have noted, we need to continually review our legislation and our market structures to ensure they keep up with the changing landscape.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This Bill is the result of our most recent round of reviews.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Ms He Ting Ru's question, MTI and EMA work on efforts to decarbonise our energy mix and transition our power sector to net-zero.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how our energy mix will change by 2050.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our energy mix in 2050 and beyond will depend on a combination of commercial, technological and geopolitical developments.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Yip suggested focusing hydrogen research efforts on domestic production of hydrogen.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Producing hydrogen domestically is unlikely to be feasible or commercially viable for now, given the need for significant amounts of domestic renewable energy resources, which we do not have.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our focus is therefore on technologies to transport and to use hydrogen or its carriers safely and cost-effectively.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As for Mr Yip's query on phasing out diesel, we may still need fuels like diesel during an emergency.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our natural gas power plants can switch to using diesel if natural gas supply is disrupted.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I think all of you know the chemistry.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Diesel can be stockpiled more easily, it is denser and is more cost effective than natural gas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition, our critical services such as hospitals and airport have diesel generators on standby in case there are disruptions to power supplies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members have asked how our decarbonisation plans will affect the cost of electricity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our approach is to harness market forces and foster competition to drive efficiency.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, power generation companies or gencos are incentivised to invest in more efficient gas turbines.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will bring down costs and thus lower electricity prices through the competitive bidding process in our wholesale market.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Nonetheless, the cost of fuel accounts for the majority of our gencos' costs and is hence the fundamental driver of electricity prices today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi also asked about the trajectory of electricity prices in the near and medium term.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This depends on which direction fuel prices move as well as on technological developments.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In the near term, natural gas will remain the primary source of energy for power generation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, electricity tariffs will continue to be driven by gas prices, which generally track global oil prices.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Geopolitical uncertainties arising from the ongoing Russia-Ukraine and Middle Eastern conflicts continue to pose risks to gas markets.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In the medium term, the share of low-carbon energy sources in our energy mix will grow.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our electricity prices will increasingly depend on the costs of these low-carbon energy sources, including those we import from regional countries.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is thus difficult to predict the trajectory of these costs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, while solar photovoltaics panel costs have fallen by 82% between 2010 and 2022, the costs of high-voltage subsea cables, or HVDC cables, that are needed to transmit electricity over long distances have risen significantly, with factories now facing production constraints.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government has always been and will always be mindful of the impact of electricity prices on Singaporeans and on businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many Members have encouraged the Government to continue supporting our lower- and middle-income households on utilities to ensure that no group is left behind in this energy transition.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In addition to support for utilities expenses, the Government provides cost of living support for all Singaporean households through the Assurance Package, which includes Community Development Council vouchers for all Singaporean households.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government understands Singaporeans' cost of living concerns and will regularly review our support measures.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Tan and Ms He emphasised the need to manage demand, even as we decarbonise our energy supplies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This helps our consumers track and make more informed decisions about their energy consumption.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will also continue helping our businesses improve energy efficiency and in turn, lower their energy costs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And in doing so, we will continue to pay special attention to supporting SMEs, which is something that Mr Neil Parekh highlighted.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But as Ms Tan and Ms He said, it is not just about energy efficiency, it is also about energy conservation, it is about using less.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I hope that we can make this a shared goal among all of us, Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members including Mr Liang Eng Hwa, Mr Don Wee, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Mark Lee and Mr Louis Ng have asked whether the new initiatives for energy security, market development and decarbonisation services will raise business costs, as well as affect the lower-income.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, the Minister for Trade and Industry must approve cost recovery rates.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Ms Jessica Tan's query on what will trigger this decision, new initiatives related to energy security, market development and decarbonisation will only be introduced if necessary for the power system.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will seek to be targeted in the implementation of these initiatives.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, as some Members suggested, entities that benefit more from an initiative could pay a higher rate so that costs are allocated fairly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, a Cost Recovery Advisory Committee of non-Government representatives will provide the Minister with independent advice on EMA's proposed rates.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As Mr Mark Lee suggested, the committee could include Members who can advise on the impact of EMA's proposed rates on businesses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Third, EMA will consult stakeholders and give reasonable notice before introducing cost recovery measures.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Where possible, EMA will implement such measures gradually, to allow time for adjustment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Louis Ng asked about the operational flexibility EMA has in imposing cost recovery rates.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The provisions allow EMA to recover costs based on "reasonable estimates" of costs payable, in addition to costs that have been paid.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is so that EMA can smoothen out the costs collected over time.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will seek to be as measured, sensitive and practical as it can, in its cost recovery measures, so as to minimise the likelihood and the magnitude of over- or under-collection.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Many Members have highlighted the importance of the FEF.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And I have explained earlier how the fund would be used.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms He Ting Ru asked about how we would measure the success of the fund.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ultimately, the fund's success is determined by whether we can achieve the energy transition in a cost effective manner while ensuring energy security.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms He also noted that the fund can be used on energy security measures and asked whether that included fossil fuel plants.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House, even as we decarbonise, we have to ensure that Singapore's energy security is not compromised.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Therefore, we should be prepared to consider all options to support a secure and sustainable energy transition.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is also how we mitigate various risks from renewable electricity imports.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Louis Ng asked how the $5 billion amount was decided and how long it would last.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is precisely why we need to start setting aside monies for it, as and when we are able to.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa asked if the FEF can fund EMA's initiatives instead of recovering costs from consumers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is to encourage efficient electricity use and prevent wastage.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Subsidising electricity is not sustainable in the long run.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Electricity prices should continue to reflect the cost of producing and supplying electricity.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Liang also asked if the fund could support nuclear energy projects.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is too early to say, because no decision has been made to deploy nuclear energy in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Ms Jessica Tan and Mr Neil Parekh asked if we have identified potential projects that are aligned with our larger energy masterplan.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The FEF complements, but it does not replace, existing funding initiatives for energy efficiency and research and development.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are worthwhile areas that the Government is already supporting.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The FEF's mandate, and I want to reiterate, is to catalyse the deployment of low-carbon energy infrastructure, including some which would otherwise have taken a very long time to commission.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, I hope that this addresses Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Yip Hon Weng and Ms He Ting Ru's questions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I would also like to assure Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Louis Ng and Ms Carrie Tan that there will be strict oversight over the fund's use.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, qualifying projects will undergo the same stringent evaluation and approval processes as any other Government infrastructure project, involving a careful evaluation of technological and commercial risks and the eventual costs of electricity generated through such low-carbon sources.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Third, the Government will employ competitive processes where possible, such as tenders and price discovery mechanisms, to ensure that energy transition projects are value-for-money.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Fourth, we will establish milestones to ensure that project timelines remain on track and that we have the flexibility to reduce abortive costs if circumstances change.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Fifth, top-ups to the fund, balances and annual outlays will be included in EMA's financial statements, which are presented to Parliament annually.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This Bill therefore reflects our careful and calibrated approach towards managing the costs of the energy transition, while supporting their investments needed to making it a reality.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Government will continue to plan and build infrastructure to meet energy needs and save up for these investments through the FEF to reduce the burden on future generations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng pointed out the risks and costs of new low-carbon technologies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The FEF will enable us to moderate the steep costs that arise from investing in nascent technologies that are strategic for Singapore's needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These are costs that consumers would otherwise have to bear.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will maintain fiscal sustainability by avoiding blanket subsidies, while continuing to help households manage electricity costs in a targeted and responsible manner.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Yip raised concerns about whether expanding EMA's powers could distort competition or create an uneven playing field.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Allow me to explain why these powers are necessary and what safeguards are in place.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To manage the uncertainties of the energy transition, we must empower EMA to plan for a net-zero energy future.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Each energy source has specific requirements and limitations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our amendments to facilitate shared access to critical energy infrastructure and introduce approval obligations for repurposing key electricity and gas assets will enable EMA to optimise the use of infrastructure in land-scarce Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA's powers will be exercised sensitively and carefully.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, EMA will consult relevant stakeholders to understand their considerations before exercising its powers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Second, specific criteria that must be met before EMA can exercise those powers.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Third, parties can appeal EMA's decisions to the Minister of Trade and Industry.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, Mr Mark Lee, Mr Louis Ng and Mr Don Wee asked how EMA's powers to facilitate shared access to critical energy infrastructure will be exercised.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Shared access allows licensees to access or connect to critical energy infrastructure owned by others to carry out their functions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, electricity importers may require access to electricity infrastructure owned by others to bring imported electricity into our domestic grid.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And yes, as Mr Mark Lee has asked, Battery Energy Storage Systems are also included as critical energy infrastructure.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Infrastructure owners and licensees should first seek to reach mutual agreement on the terms of shared access, including fair compensation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Minister will appoint Members with relevant expertise to the Appeal Panel.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As far as possible, the Minister will appoint Members who are accepted by both parties to the shared access agreement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Mr Louis Ng's query, the shared access agreements entered into by both parties are legally binding contracts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These should include provisions for compensation in case of losses that are mutually agreed to by both parties, or determined by an Appeal Panel.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Don Wee asked if EMA's powers to approve the repurposing of electricity and gas assets might limit companies' agility in responding to market changes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will only reject requests if repurposing undermines energy security and reliability.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will strike a balance between the commercial needs for the potential repurposing, while ensuring that energy security and system reliability in land-scarce Singapore will not be compromised.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Specific approvals timelines are not set in legislation, due to the different circumstances for each case.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Companies should engage EMA early, on any potential repurposing, and EMA will assess the cases promptly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Mr Saktiandi’s questions, the approval obligation for repurposing of key electricity and gas assets applies to relevant facilities and installations which are specified in legislation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: No particular incident sparked concern about repurposing key energy assets but we have to plan for such a possibility, especially due to Singapore’s land constraints.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Next, Members asked about the need to centralise gas procurement under a central gas entity, which we will call Gasco for now.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: During the 2021 and 2022 global energy crisis, governments struggled to secure fuel supplies and manage price spikes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Beyond crisis measures, EMA subsequently strengthened our market structure by centralising the process for new generation investments, enhancing regulatory protections for consumers and implementing a Temporary Price Cap to curb wholesale market volatility.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Allow me to reiterate what we seek to accomplish by establishing the Gasco.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: First, the Gasco enhances our gas supply security.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our current market-based gas procurement system does not provide sufficient assurance of adequate gas supply to meet our needs at the national level, especially during volatile market conditions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: During the energy crisis, gencos were unwilling to contract more gas because of the highly volatile prices.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We were, therefore, at risk of being short of gas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In October 2021, when a whole confluence of factors caused the prices of natural gas to spike, we quickly set up a SLF.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Members of the House, that proved prescient, especially when the Russian-Ukraine war broke out in February 2022 and it threw the global gas market into turmoil.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our gencos, currently, import most of our gas from neighbouring countries, such as Indonesia, Malaysia and Australia.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With the Gasco, we will seek to broaden our sources of supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Mr Saktiandi’s question, instead of capping the amount from any single source, we seek to have a well-diversified gas portfolio.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This diversity in terms of sources and contract length increases our protection against supply chain disruptions, and mitigates the risks of over-centralisation and a single point of failure, something which Mr Don Wee spoke about.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Third, the Gasco allows us to enter into long-term contracts that provide more stable prices and certainty of supply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our current market-based approach does not sufficiently reward gencos that commit to long-term contracts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, let us say Genco A signs a 20-year contract for gas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If gas prices come down, other gencos can undercut Genco A by using cheaper gas.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Genco A will be at risk of making large losses.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, you can appreciate why our gencos are reluctant to enter into such long-term contracts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Moving forward, because our gencos can only buy gas from the Gasco and will be required to buy sufficient amounts of gas, this reduces the risks of any genco being undercut by other gencos as a result of long-term contracts.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Centralisation and scale therefore give the Gasco room to negotiate for more favourable gas contracting terms, as well as to explore co-procurement with other major gas procurement entities, such as JERA of Japan and KOGAS of Korea.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked who the Gasco will be and how it will be run.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Gasco’s primary objective is to procure and supply gas to meet Singapore’s power generation needs, not to maximise profits.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Gasco will be staffed by professionals who will take a long-term, systems-view to guide the gas procurement.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It will also align its gas portfolio to national needs, accounting for our electricity demand growth and decarbonisation plans.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: To Mr Liang Eng Hwa's question, this regulated fee will be approved and transparently published by EMA.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will regulate the Gasco to ensure that the gas procurement framework improves the security and the resilience of Singapore’s natural gas supply to the power sector, while keeping prices competitive.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This will be a delicate balance and it will require the Gasco to be structured, to be resourced, incentivised and assessed accordingly.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope this addresses Ms Jessica Tan’s question.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We appreciate Mr Saktiandi’s suggestion to give gencos the flexibility to source for gas supplies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In fact, EMA is working with gencos to develop a mechanism that incentivises them to refer competitively-priced gas supplies to the Gasco for evaluation and potential incorporation into its portfolio.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singaporeans and businesses are understandably concerned about the prospect of power rationing, even though most recognise the need for doing so during emergencies.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is understandable, since electricity is crucial for our daily routines and for the economy.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I want to reassure Members that power rationing will only be as a last resort.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have existing measures to mitigate the impact of gas supply disruptions.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our LNG terminal can support our natural gas demand even if piped natural gas is disrupted.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have sufficient generation capacity, including a 27% reserve margin which provides for planned and unplanned outages.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These measures, combined with voluntary power conservation, can meet all our demand in most potential disruption scenarios.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The disruptions to the Nord Stream gas pipelines connecting Russia and Europe in September 2022, highlight the vulnerability of energy infrastructure to geopolitical tensions and how quickly energy supplies can be disrupted.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: These amendments for power rationing are, therefore, necessary for the worst-case scenario as a matter of national security.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Don Wee, Mr Mark Lee and Mr Neil Parekh asked what constitutes an emergency that justifies power rationing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For example, a severe fuel shortage could trigger such an emergency.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Mark Lee and Mr Neil Parekh asked for timely communication with companies about the initiation, duration and cessation of these measures.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: EMA will strive to notify affected parties through various channels before implementing power rationing, so that they have time to safely reduce or power down operations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: However, our priority during an emergency would be to implement power rationing expeditiously to ensure system stability.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The duration may not be known upfront, as it will depend on the nature of the emergency.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But EMA will lift power rationing once it is no longer required.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Mr Don Wee also asked how EMA will ensure that rationing measures are proportionate and do not unduly disrupt economic activities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We appreciate Ms Carrie Tan and Mr Neil Parekh's suggestion to run power rationing simulations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Earlier this year, organisations across Singapore simulated power, water or food supply disruptions as part of Total Defence Day activities.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will continue to find new ways to engage the public on our energy story as well as support business continuity planning.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Like every nation on this energy transition journey, Singapore is grappling with the “energy trilemma” – how to realise an energy future that is secure, that is cost-competitive and sustainable.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For our beloved country Singapore, the stakes are even higher.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But, then again, the stakes for our little red dot have always been higher.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Energy is an existential challenge that defines this generation.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This Bill, Members of the House, takes us closer to securing our clean energy future by ensuring that our energy system is resilient, adaptable and ready for the transition and transformation ahead.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This is not something that the Government can do alone.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Let us all work together with businesses, to innovate commercially viable low-carbon solutions; and with our consumers to support our energy story, use energy prudently and even as all of us in Government seek to keep costs in check.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We all know, we have heard so many Members of the House speak earlier on, about our Water Story.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We all know our Water Story well and how Singapore turned scarcity into strength.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Now, I call upon all of us: write the net zero chapter of our Singapore Energy Story.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is your story, it is our children’s and grandchildren’s stories.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Let us innovate, let us adapt and work towards our clean energy future together.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Once again, I thank Members for your strong support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there any clarifications for Minister from any Member?

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Dr Tan, it looks like you did a very good wrapping-up speech.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 4.03 pm until 4.25 pm.
